reasons: Lake identity verifies United States v. Chadwick, U.S. Supreme Court, decided 1977-06-21, year 1977.
Lake citations list official 433 U.S. 1, parallels 97 S. Ct. 2476 and 53 L. Ed. 2d 538, and 1977 U.S. LEXIS 133.

defect.evidence_quote: In sum, a person’s expectations of privacy in personal luggage are substantially greater than in an automobile.
defect.problem: The holding is substantively supported except that 'Luggage/containers carry a high expectation of privacy' is broader than Chadwick's own text. The opinion speaks about personal effects in a double-locked footlocker, personal luggage, and other personal property not immediately associated with the arrestee, not all containers categorically.
defect.proposed_fix: Narrow the opening to locked luggage/personal effects, or containers used as repositories of personal effects, rather than 'luggage/containers' generally.

reasons: The warrant/no-exigency part is supported by the text saying the footlocker was under exclusive control and it was unreasonable to search without a warrant.
The SIA part is supported by the text saying secured luggage or personal property is no longer an incident of arrest once access/danger is gone.
The disclosed opinion does not support the unqualified breadth of 'containers' as a standalone category.
residual_risks: Later treatment language also uses 'luggage/containers', but Lens A support for Chadwick's own holding is narrower.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Locked luggage or personal effects carry a high expectation of privacy; once such property is reduced to exclusive police control with no exigency, Chadwick requires a warrant and rejects SIA.

reasons: The opinion decides whether agents needed a warrant before opening a locked footlocker lawfully seized at arrest.
The text treats the footlocker as an effect/personal property and draws the warrant line when property comes under exclusive police dominion with no exigency.
residual_risks: 'Key — Anchor' is partly a corpus role judgment, but the opinion's direct subject matter supports it.

reasons: The opinion directly analyzes search incident to arrest, immediate control, weapons, and destructible evidence.
It holds the search was not incident to arrest once the footlocker was secured and respondents were in custody, supporting a cross-doctrine SIA role.
The opinion directly addresses the automobile-exception analogy and says the footlocker's brief contact with the car did not make it an automobile search.
The lake treatment scope note and point override identify Acevedo as limiting Chadwick in the auto-container setting.
residual_risks: The body 'Appears on' line labels Automobile Exception as 'Key — Limiting / Historical' while the inventory/frontmatter says 'Related'; that role-strength mismatch is outside this assertion's payload but should be normalized.

reasons: Treatment merits are outside Lens A, so this is not a treatment/currency finding.

The disclosed lake and content frontmatter contain the same point, point label, caution status, provisional binding status, and Acevedo entry with cite 500 U.S. 565, cluster_id 112608, field_ii limited.
residual_risks: Lens B should audit whether the treatment characterization is legally current.

reasons: Treatment merits are outside Lens A, so this is not a treatment/currency finding.
The lake treatment record and content frontmatter match the asserted caution status, dates, migration-seed basis, varies_by_point flag, and scope note.
residual_risks: Lens B should audit the legal treatment and the page's textual 'limited' display against field_i_validity caution.

The content page asserts authority_weight 'Binding — SCOTUS', matching the disclosed court identity.
